topic: Using concentrations of solutions in mol/dm 3 (chemistry only) (HT only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: A bottle of dilute hydrochloric acid is labelled 0.500 mol/dm³. What does this label tell you about the solution inside?
items.correct: Every 1 dm³ of this solution contains 0.500 mol of hydrogen chloride.
items.misconception: Every 1 dm³ of this solution contains 0.500 g of hydrogen chloride.
items.why: Both units end in '/dm³', which makes them look like alternative labels for one quantity, in the way that 'cm' and 'centimetre' are. Students also meet the two units in the same lesson and copy one number into both columns of a table. Moles and grams measure different things, so the two concentrations are different numbers. Concentration in g/dm³ = concentration in mol/dm³ × relative formula mass.
items.random_wrong: Every 1 cm³ of this solution holds 0.500 mol of hydrogen chloride.

items.q: Solution P contains 0.0400 mol of potassium hydroxide in 200 cm³ of solution. Solution Q contains 0.0400 mol of potassium hydroxide in 500 cm³ of solution. Which statement about their concentrations in mol/dm³ is correct?
items.correct: P is the more concentrated, as the same amount of solute sits in less solution.
items.misconception: Q is the more concentrated, because it contains the larger volume of solution overall.
items.why: A larger volume looks like 'more solution and therefore more of everything'. Students treat concentration as directly proportional to volume instead of inversely proportional to it. For a fixed amount of solute, concentration falls as volume rises. Double the volume and the concentration halves.
items.random_wrong: P and Q are equally concentrated, since each of them holds 0.0400 mol of solute.

items.q: What amount, in moles, of sodium hydroxide is present in 250 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.200 mol/dm³?
items.why: The volume in the question is given in cm³ and the conversion leaves no trace in the written working, so it is the step most often skipped under time pressure. A concentration in mol/dm³ must be used with a volume in dm³. Divide the volume in cm³ by 1000 first.

items.q: What mass of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in 200 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution of concentration 0.250 mol/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)
items.why: The conversion in the other direction, mass ÷ relative formula mass = moles, is met first and practised hardest, so it is reproduced whichever way round the question runs. Moles to grams is a multiplication: mass = amount in moles × relative formula mass. Only grams to moles is a division.

items.q: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution was neutralised by exactly 20.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.100 mol/dm³. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution?
items.why: Finding the moles is the hardest step and so feels like the answer. The final division looks like tidying up, and the unit on the answer is not checked against the unit the question asked for. Moles and mol/dm³ are different quantities. After the mole ratio step, always divide by the volume in dm³ of the solution whose concentration is wanted.

items.q: In a titration, 20.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide solution was neutralised by exactly 25.0 cm³ of sulfuric acid of concentration 0.0500 mol/dm³. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution?
items.why: The volume in the question is given in cm³ and the conversion leaves no trace in the written working, so it is the step most often skipped under time pressure. A concentration in mol/dm³ must be used with a volume in dm³. Divide the volume in cm³ by 1000 first.

items.q: 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide is dissolved in water and the solution is made up to 250 cm³. What is the concentration of the solution in mol/dm³? (Relative formula mass of NaOH = 40)
items.why: The volume in the question is given in cm³ and the conversion leaves no trace in the written working, so it is the step most often skipped under time pressure. A concentration in mol/dm³ must be used with a volume in dm³. Divide the volume in cm³ by 1000 first.

items.q: A student adds 250 cm³ of water to 250 cm³ of sodium chloride solution of concentration 0.800 mol/dm³ and stirs. What happens to the concentration, and why?
items.correct: It halves to 0.400 mol/dm³, because the same amount of solute is now in twice the volume.
items.misconception: It stays at 0.800 mol/dm³, because no sodium chloride has been added to it or taken from it.
items.why: 'Concentration' is heard as 'how much stuff is dissolved'. Because the amount of solute is conserved when water is added, students conclude that the concentration must be conserved too. Concentration is the amount of solute divided by the volume of solution. Both parts matter, so changing the volume changes the concentration even when the amount of solute is fixed.
items.random_wrong: It doubles to 1.60 mol/dm³, because the volume of the solution has been doubled.

items.q: A solution is 0.500 mol/dm³. How much solute is dissolved in 1 cm³ of it?
items.correct: 0.000500 mol, because 1 cm³ is one thousandth of 1 dm³.
items.misconception: mol/dm³ states the amount of solute in each cm³ of solution, because cm³ is the volume unit used in the laboratory.
items.why: Nearly every volume a student measures in a school laboratory is in cm³, so the cm³ in front of them displaces the dm³ printed in the unit on the bottle when they read the label. Read the unit as written: mol per dm³ means moles in each 1 dm³, and 1 dm³ is 1000 cm³ of solution.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: 0.100 mol of a solid is stirred into 1 dm³ of water and dissolves. Is the concentration exactly 0.100 mol/dm³?
items.correct: Not necessarily. Concentration uses the volume of the final solution, which is not the same thing as the 1 dm³ of water taken.
items.misconception: The volume in a concentration is the volume of water added to dissolve the solute.
items.why: Students picture making a solution as 'solid plus water', so the water is the volume they remember measuring, and the fact that a solution is made up to a fixed final volume in a volumetric flask is lost. Concentration in mol/dm³ is the amount of solute divided by the volume of the solution, measured after the solution has been made up.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.misconception: There are 100 cm³ in 1 dm³, because there are 10 cm in a decimetre.
items.why: The length conversion 1 dm = 10 cm is remembered and applied directly without being cubed, and 100 feels like a familiar conversion factor for units that differ by a factor of ten. 1 dm = 10 cm, so 1 dm³ = 10³ cm³ = 1000 cm³. Divide a volume in cm³ by 1000 to get dm³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: 4.0 g of a solute is made up to 250 cm³ of solution. Is the concentration 16 mol/dm³?
items.correct: No. Convert the mass into moles first by dividing by the relative formula mass, then divide by the volume in dm³.
items.misconception: Concentration in mol/dm³ is the mass of solute in grams divided by the volume of the solution.
items.why: Students remember 'concentration is stuff divided by volume' and reach for the number they were given, which is a mass. The relative formula mass step is dropped because the unit on the answer is not read. The top of the division must be an amount in moles: moles = mass ÷ relative formula mass, then concentration = moles ÷ volume in dm³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Concentration = amount ÷ volume. How is the amount of solute in a given volume found from it?
items.misconception: The relationship can be rearranged as amount = concentration ÷ volume, or as volume ÷ amount, since it is a division either way.
items.why: The relationship is memorised as 'a division' rather than as a rearrangement, so the two quantities are combined in whichever order produces a tidy looking number on the calculator. From c = n ÷ V it follows that n = c × V and V = n ÷ c. Check any rearrangement by checking the unit of the answer it produces.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH solution is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ HCl. Is c(NaOH) = 0.100 × 25.0 ÷ 20.0?
items.correct: No. That uses the volumes the wrong way round. c(NaOH) = 0.100 × 20.0 ÷ 25.0 = 0.0800 mol/dm³.
items.misconception: The known concentration can be scaled by the ratio of the two volumes taken in whichever order they appear in the question.
items.why: Students shortcut the two-step method into a single ratio without tracking which volume belongs to which solution, and the first volume printed in the question becomes the top of the fraction. Work in steps: amount in moles of the solution of known concentration from its own volume, then the mole ratio, then divide by the volume in dm³ of the other solution.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. If 0.00125 mol of H₂SO₄ reacts completely, what amount of NaOH reacts with it?
items.correct: 0.00250 mol, because 1 mol of H₂SO₄ reacts with 2 mol of NaOH.
items.misconception: Solutions that react completely contain equal amounts in moles, so the balanced equation does not have to be used.
items.why: The first titrations students meet are acid and alkali in a 1 : 1 ratio, so 'moles of acid = moles of alkali' becomes the remembered rule and survives into questions where the ratio is not 1 : 1. Read the balancing numbers in the equation and use them to convert between the two amounts before dividing by the volume.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
